thread.title: Apple Watch is safe, but China tariffs could still hit other consumer tech products

author: morningstar.com
title: Apple Watch is safe, but China tariffs could still hit other consumer tech products

organizations.name: office of the u.s. trade representative

text:
By Therese Poletti, MarketWatch
Tariffs 'will stifle our global leadership in 5G, create an internet tax on businesses and cause uncertainty for companies,' CTA says
While Apple Inc. and the smartwatch business is safe from the latest tariffs the Trump administration enacted against China, there are many other potential areas of tech that could be hurt by the levies on $200 billion in Chinese goods (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trump-to-impose-another-200-billion-in-tariffs-on-chinese-goods-2018-09-17).
Late Monday, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative issued a final list of goods that will be subject to an initial 10% tariff, beginning Sept. 24, and then rising to 25% in January. While some products developed by Apple Inc.(AAPL) and Fitbit Inc. (FIT) were spared, after smartwatches and wireless earbuds were removed from the list at the 11th hour, (https://www.wsj.com/articles/for-apple-u-s-china-trade-fight-grows-riskier-1537188213)other products -- such as those that use printed circuit-board assemblies, for example -- appear to be subject to tariffs.
Read also: Apple and other companies sound alarm on Trump's trade war (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-and-other-tech-companies-sound-the-alarm-on-trumps-china-tariff-plans-2018-09-11)
In a brief statement late Monday, the Consumer Technology Association said that it appreciates the Trump administration's removal of some consumer devices from the tariff list. However, the tech trade group that runs CES said it was especially worried about retaliatory tariffs, especially those on printed-circuit assemblies and networking equipment, which could hurt future investment into 5G, the next-generation telecommunications standard.
"Retaliatory tariffs, whether 10% or 25%, are bad policy," CTA president and CEO Gary Shapiro said in a statement. "We are especially concerned about retaliatory tariffs on printed-circuit assemblies, routers and networking equipment. They will stifle our global leadership in 5G, create an internet tax on businesses and cause uncertainty for companies."
In addition, the CTA said that the retaliatory tariffs against China may also violate the law: "Congress has not given the president or the USTR a blank check to pursue a trade war. These new retaliatory tariffs run afoul of the carefully tailored provisions of the Trade Act of 1974."
A CTA spokeswoman was not available to comment further on the statement.
In the lead-up to the latest tariffs, chip giant Intel Corp.(INTC) wrote a letter last week (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-and-other-tech-companies-sound-the-alarm-on-trumps-china-tariff-plans-2018-09-11)as part of the public comment period, saying that "the proposed List 3 is a game changer for the American consumer -- especially if the tariffs are increased from 10% to 25%."
The company's global policy officer, Gary Pearson, noted in his letter that a "wide array of technology products and parts will now be subject to tariffs if List 3 is finalized as is."
According to the most recent list issued by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=USTR-2018-0026-0001), while smartwatches have been removed, digital processing units, transmission devices, television cameras, digital cameras, printed-circuit assemblies and parts of automatic data-processing machines are among the broader technologies to still be subject to tariffs.
Intel said the list was "so broad and encompasses so many information, communication and technology products that significant consumer harm is unavoidable." An Intel spokesman said the company did not have any immediate comment on the news late Monday.
During the hearings, which had to be extended to accommodate the large number of companies that wanted to testify, the CTA said that tariffs on printed-circuit assemblies could affect cell phones, flat-panel TVs, laptops, electronic calculators and home appliances. Even if companies make their products in the U.S. or in another country, many have them assembled in China and shipped back to the U.S. for sale.
"Many of the components on this list are building blocks of future technologies," the CTA said in its testimony in Washington last month. "Internet of Things, AI, machine learning, 5G, these will all become more expensive and leave less money for companies to invest research into research and development."
Networking and data centers also appear to be affected by tariffs on what is described in the list (https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-tariffs/u-s-duties-spare-apple-gadgets-but-hit-cloud-industry-idUSKCN1LX27W)as "machines for the reception, conversion and transmission or regeneration of voice, images or other data, including switching and routing appa[rata]." (https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-tariffs/u-s-duties-spare-apple-gadgets-but-hit-cloud-industry-idUSKCN1LX27W)
Trump's latest batch of tariffs are expected to lead to higher prices to a wide range of consumer electronics. Companies also now risk further retaliation from China, which could hurt even more products, since China is a significant part of the global supply and manufacturing chain.
"All of those ODMs [original device manufacturers] will be influenced by the Chinese government," said Mark Vena, a senior analyst at Moor Insights. "If the Chinese were to restrict supply in a significant way, that's going to be a ratcheting up of things, it's kind of like going to Defcon 2."
-Therese Poletti; 17-18 2225ET
